d.title: Safe and idempotent are two different promises, and PATCH keeps neither
d.caption: **Safe means no side effects at all, so a crawler or a browser prefetch cannot break anything. Idempotent means doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once** — which is what makes a retry safe after a lost response. The two rows worth internalising: **`DELETE` is idempotent, so deleting twice is not an error and returning 404 on the second call is a design choice rather than a requirement** — and **`PATCH` is not idempotent by default**, because `{"quantity": "+1"}` applied twice is not the same as once.

d.title: One row is a production incident waiting: requests has no default timeout
d.caption: **`requests` waits forever by default and `httpx` stops at 5 seconds** — which is the difference between a slow upstream degrading your service and a slow upstream exhausting your thread pool. Everything else is a preference; that row is a defect you must remember to patch at every call site. The rest favours `httpx` for new code: **the same API with an `AsyncClient`, HTTP/2 behind one flag** — against `requests`' one real advantage, **ubiquity: every example on the internet uses it.**

d.title: Two boundaries in one class: exceptions and types
d.caption: **Callers never see `requests` or the vendor's field names — so swapping the HTTP library, or absorbing a renamed field, is a change inside one file.** The exception half is the one people skip: **a client that lets `requests.HTTPError` escape has made its callers depend on `requests`**, so every `except` clause upstream is now coupled to a library choice. Translate at the boundary: **the vendor's 429 becomes your `RateLimited`, their JSON becomes your dataclass, and their outage becomes one exception type you can retry on.**

nodes.label: So callers never import requests
nodes.sub: nor know a field was renamed

nodes.label: And swapping the library is one file

d.title: Seven places a rule can live, and the fast ones run in Rust
d.caption: **`Field(ge=1)`, a pattern and an `Enum` all run in Rust — so prefer them, and not only for speed: they appear in the generated OpenAPI schema where a custom validator does not.** The ordering is the content: **`mode="before"` runs on the raw value, so it is where you normalise; a plain `field_validator` runs after coercion, so it sees the typed value.** And the row people reach for too late: **a rule spanning two fields must be a `model_validator(mode="after")`**, because a field validator cannot see its siblings.

state: in Rust, and in the schema

d.title: `Field(exclude=True)` and `SecretStr` are the two that prevent incidents
d.caption: **A `password_hash` in a `model_dump()` reaches a log line, a response body or an analytics payload — and the model is where that is prevented once rather than at every serialisation site.** The two work differently and both are worth having: **`exclude=True` keeps the field out of the dump entirely, and `SecretStr` keeps the value out of `repr()` and any accidental interpolation** while leaving it readable through `.get_secret_value()`. Which is the general point: **validation and serialisation are separate contracts, and the input model is rarely the right output model.**

nodes.label: So a hash reaches a log or a response
In and out are different contracts

d.title: The point is that it fails at startup
d.caption: **A missing or malformed environment variable stops the process immediately, with the field name in the message** — rather than producing an `AttributeError` on `None` at 3am, in the one code path that reads it. Which reframes what a settings class is for: **it is not configuration plumbing, it is a startup-time assertion that the deployment is complete.** And the corollary: **anything read with `os.environ.get(...)` scattered through the code is a variable that can be missing without anybody noticing until it is used.**

nodes.sub: in the one path that reads it

d.title: The breaking-change check is the one worth adding first
d.caption: **`oasdiff` in CI turns “we think this is backward compatible” into a build that fails when it is not** — which is the only mechanism in the lesson that catches a removed field or a narrowed type before a client does. The generated schema is the input that makes it possible: **because the models *are* the contract, the OpenAPI document cannot drift from the code**, so a diff between two commits' schemas is a diff of the real API. **And the client generators are downstream of the same file**, so a breaking change shows up as a compile error in a typed client.

nodes.label: oasdiff in CI
nodes.sub: compares it to the last release

nodes.label: A removed field fails the build
And a typed client gets a compile error

d.title: `lifespan` replaced the startup and shutdown events
d.caption: **One async context manager around the application's whole life: everything before the `yield` is startup and everything after is shutdown** — which is 5.8's context-manager shape at application scope, and it fixes the thing the old decorators could not express: **a resource whose setup and teardown belong together, like a connection pool, is now one function rather than two that must be kept in sync.** And the ordering guarantee matters: **shutdown runs in reverse, so the pool closes before the thing that registered it.**

nodes.label: So a pool is ONE function
on_event could not express that
nodes.sub: which is why it was replaced

d.title: The override is by object, not by import path
d.caption: **`app.dependency_overrides[get_db] = fake_db` keys on the function object itself — so moving `get_db` to another module does not break the test**, which is the failure mode of every `@patch("app.routes.get_db")` string. That is the payoff of declaring dependencies rather than importing them: **the test substitutes the same object the route asked for, with no knowledge of where either lives.** And it composes: **overriding a dependency replaces it for every route that depends on it, including transitively**, so one line can substitute a database for the whole suite.

nodes.label: And applies transitively
nodes.sub: one line for the whole suite

d.title: A background task runs in the same process, with no retry and no durability
d.caption: **`BackgroundTasks` runs after the response in the same process — so a restart between the response and the task loses it silently**, and the client has already been told the work succeeded. Which makes the decision rule sharp rather than a preference: **use it for work whose loss is acceptable — a cache warm, a metric, a best-effort notification — and a real queue for anything a user would complain about losing.** The giveaway question: **if this task never ran, would anyone open a ticket?**

nodes.label: And the client was told it succeeded
Fine for a cache warm or a metric

d.title: Five procedure names, and each resource version answers a question the verb could not
d.caption: **`POST /cancelOrder` is a verb with no address; `POST /orders/{id}/cancellation` makes cancellation a thing you can also `GET`** — which is the test for the whole list: does the noun have state worth retrieving later? The clearest pair is the last: **an approval has a who and a when worth returning**, so `POST /orders/{id}/approvals` gives you a record and `POST /approve` gives you nothing. And **`GET /users/{id}/orders` is cacheable, safe and prefetchable** where a `POST` is none of those.

state: an approval has a who and a when

d.title: Fetching `limit + 1` tells you there is a next page without a COUNT
d.caption: **A second `COUNT(*)` query on a large table is the expensive part of pagination, and asking for one row more than you need answers the same question** — if you got `limit + 1` back, there is another page, and you return the first `limit`. The cursor argument follows from the same table: **offset pagination makes the database skip every row it is not returning, so page 5,000 scans 100,000 rows to discard them** — and a keyset cursor on an indexed column is constant cost at every depth, **at the price of no random page access.**

nodes.label: OFFSET makes the DB skip rows
A keyset cursor is constant cost
At the price of no random page

d.title: Steps 3 and 4 are what separate a deprecation from an outage
d.caption: **Without usage data, removal is a guess** — and the client you did not know about is the one that breaks. So the sequence is: announce, add a `Deprecation` header and a sunset date, **then instrument the old path per client so you can see who is still calling it**, and **contact them with their own numbers** rather than a changelog entry. Only then remove. The step people skip is the third, **because it requires having built per-client attribution before you needed it** — which is 6.4's correlation id earning its place a second time.

nodes.label: 1-2. Announce, and send a Deprecation header
3. Instrument the old path PER CLIENT
4. Contact them with their own numbers

d.title: Document at-least-once delivery explicitly
d.caption: **A receiver that assumes exactly-once will double-process the first time you retry a webhook** — and you will retry, because a timeout cannot distinguish a lost request from a slow response. So the contract has to say so, and give them what they need to cope: **a stable event id to deduplicate on, a signature over the raw body so they can verify it, and a timestamp so they can reject a replay.** The sending side's obligations are the mirror image: **sign the raw bytes rather than re-serialised JSON, retry with backoff, and stop after a bounded number of attempts.**

nodes.label: A timeout cannot tell lost from slow
And a timestamp, to reject replays

d.title: Revocation is the row that decides it
d.caption: **A server session is revoked by deleting a row, immediately. A JWT cannot be revoked until it expires — unless you add a store, at which point you have a session with extra steps.** That is why **a first-party web application wants sessions**: logging someone out has to work. JWTs win where there is no shared store to consult: **service-to-service, and short-lived access tokens where the expiry *is* the revocation window.** And the cost is on every request: **several hundred bytes on the wire, with everything in it visible to the holder.**

d.title: Six rules, and two of them are about places people forget are readable
d.caption: **A secret in a Docker `ENV` is in a readable image layer, and a secret in a URL is logged by every proxy, browser history and access log between you and the server** — both feel private and neither is. The last two are about time rather than placement: **the same secret in every environment means staging can touch production**, and **a secret that has never rotated cannot be rotated in an emergency** — which is why the rotation schedule matters less than supporting **two valid keys at once.**

state: an env var, or a secret manager

d.title: Three numbers shape the whole design, and they fall out of arithmetic
d.caption: **700,000 reads a second means the database cannot serve reads directly — cache aggressively and add read replicas. 66 TB a year, 330 TB over five, means one database cannot hold it — shard. And 210 MB/s of reads means a CDN and an object store for anything larger than text.** None of that required a design discussion; **it fell out of multiplying a user count by a per-user rate**, which is why the estimate comes before the architecture rather than justifying it afterwards.

d.title: Three API styles, and two details the reference calls interview-critical
d.caption: **Idempotency: a client that retries a POST must not create two orders — accept an `Idempotency-Key` header, store the key with the first response, and replay that response for a repeat.** And **pagination: offset makes the database skip every row it is not returning, so deep pages get slower**, where a cursor does not. The styles themselves split on cost: **REST over- and under-fetches, gRPC needs tooling and has poor browser support, and GraphQL moves the N+1 problem onto your server and makes caching harder.**

d.title: Neither helps across app instances, and a Redis lock needs a token
d.caption: **Optimistic retries under contention; pessimistic waits and deadlocks if two rows are locked in different orders** — and the choice is simply how often conflicts happen. The row that catches people is the third: **a lock in one process is invisible to another, so neither mechanism survives horizontal scaling.** A distributed lock is the answer, with two non-optional details: **a TTL so a crashed holder cannot lock forever, and a token so only the holder that owns it can release** — without the token, a slow holder deletes someone else's lock.

state: TTL: a crash cannot lock forever
or you delete someone else's lock

d.title: The four golden signals, and a correlation id on every line
d.caption: **Latency, traffic, errors and saturation — four metrics that between them answer “is it working and will it keep working”**, where saturation is the one that predicts rather than reports. Beneath them: **structured logs with a correlation id on every line** (6.4's `ContextVar`), **and traces that follow one request across services.** The ordering is worth noting: **logs tell you what happened to one request, metrics tell you what is happening to all of them, and traces tell you where the time went** — and a system with only one of the three can answer only one kind of question.

nodes.label: One of the three answers one question
nodes.sub: which is why you need all three

d.title: 47.6 ns against 44.8 ns, and that difference is the vulnerability
d.caption: **`==` on two strings returns as soon as a byte differs — so a comparison failing at byte 1 is faster than one failing at byte 16, and an attacker who can measure the difference recovers the secret one byte at a time.** The measured gap on 32-character tokens is **47.6 ns against 44.8 ns**, which is small, noisy, and exactly the kind of signal that averages out over enough requests. **`hmac.compare_digest` takes the same time whatever the inputs**, which is why it exists and why `==` on a token is a defect rather than a style choice.

d.title: For a machine caller there is no user to log in
d.caption: **An API key is a random token handed to the caller and stored hashed on your side like a password** — sent in a header, compared with `compare_digest`, scoped and revocable. Which is the whole design, and the hashing is the part people skip: **a key stored in plaintext means a database read is a full compromise of every caller.** OAuth2 client credentials is the heavier option and buys one specific thing: **the calling service authenticates once and gets a short-lived token, so a leaked credential expires on its own.**

d.title: Six layers, and the CSRF row explains why one auth scheme needs no CSRF defence at all
d.caption: **A bearer token in a header is immune, because the browser does not attach it automatically** — CSRF exists precisely because cookies are sent on any request to the origin. So the defence is scoped to cookie-authenticated state changes: **`SameSite` plus a synchroniser token compared with `compare_digest`.** The row most often misconfigured is CORS: **never `*` with credentials** — and the one most often omitted entirely is the host check, **which is what stops a poisoned `Host` header being used to build an absolute URL in a password-reset email.**
